thread.title_full: Judge rules Elon Musk must sit for depositions in lawsuits against DOGE - NewsBreak

author: Peter Rubinstein
title: Judge rules Elon Musk must sit for depositions in lawsuits against DOGE - NewsBreak
text:
By Peter Rubinstein ,
1 hours ago A federal judge on Tuesday ruled that Elon Musk and State Department officials must attend depositions over their work to dismantle the U.S. Agency for International Development (USAID) in 2025.
Though Musk was not elected to an official position within the federal government, his leadership at the Department of Government Efficiency saw a gutting of the decades-old agency without significant oversight . USAID's former workforce of 10,000 handled $43 billion in appropriations and assisted with disaster relief and economic development for some 130 countries in 2023.
The order comes as a positive step for the anonymous USAID employees who sued Musk and the department over what they have called an illegal effort to strip the agency, citing previous rulings that Musk lacked official approval or formal authority to do so. According to a report in The Lancet last July, Musk's work could lead to more than 14 million deaths over the next five years, about 4.5 million of which would be children under 5 years old.
• Trump threatens to shred Constitution for third term and admits possibility is 'exciting'
• DOJ lawyer who told judge 'this job sucks' removed from immigration assignment in Minnesota
The report in the peer-reviewed medical journal calculated the lives saved by USAID efforts over a 21-year period, and the number of lives that might be lost without them in the future.
In March 2025, Secretary of State Marco Rubio announced he was canceling 83% of USAID programs because they failed to serve "the core national interests of the United States." The funding cuts led to the closure of health clinics and food kitchens in underserved countries, and delayed or stopped the distribution of lifesaving medicine, bed nets to limit the spread of malaria, nutritional supplements for starving children, and chlorine tablets for disinfecting soiled water.
The report found that between 2001 and 2021, USAID programs prevented about 92 million deaths across 133 countries. These included 25 million deaths from HIV/AIDS, 11 million from diarrheal diseases, 8 million from malaria and 5 million from tuberculosis, according to NBC News .
According to Amira Albert Roess, professor of global health and epidemiology at George Mason University, the speed at which funding was stripped from USAID programs is partly to blame for the high death forecast.
“For better or for worse, some of the USAID-funded clinics in some areas, they were the main source of care,” she said. “If you wanted to reduce USAID funding, it could have been done in a more gradual manner, instead of this sudden — and really, in a lot of places, overnight — shuttering of clinics.”
U.S. District Judge Theodore Chuang wrote in his memorandum order that there is "no alternative" to the in-person depositions. He referenced the plaintiffs' inability to acquire information through lower-ranking officials, who failed to answer deposition requests.
Trump last February told reporters USAID was run by "a bunch of radical lunatics, and we're getting them out."
Musk, writing on his social media platform X, wrote, " USAID is a criminal organization. Time for it to die."

In December, months after Musk was ousted from his unofficial position amid a battle of public insults and accusations with President Donald Trump on social media, he called his work at the helm of DOGE only "somewhat successful."
"We were a little bit successful. We stopped a lot of funding that really just made no sense, that was just entirely wasteful," he said on a podcast with Katie Miller, wife of Trump's closest White House ally and leading policy architect Stephen Miller.
In addition to gutting USAID, DOGE slashed consumer protections and fired thousands of federal workers, many without any explanation. The department also worked to centralize data collected on American citizens, which previously had, by design, been separated across different agencies.
Government watchdogs have said the move likely violated data collection rules under the Privacy Act.
